clue.text: Where Lodovico was welcomed and embraced by fancy Prussian

indicators.note: something embraced is held inside, so the answer sits within the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A Venetian envoy is greeted warmly and hugged by an elegant German.
explanation.walkthrough: In Othello, Lodovico arrives from Venice in CYPRUS, where Othello is governor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mediterranean island is the setting of most of Shakespeare's Othello, so it is the place that visitor reached.

clue.text: Swift beasts giving joyous cries

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the brutish humanoid creatures in Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels

explanation.surface: Fast-running animals are letting out happy shrieks.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift is the satirist Jonathan Swift, not an adjective meaning fast.
explanation.definitionFit: The savage creatures ruled by horses in Gulliver's fourth voyage bear this name, which also serves as an exclamation of glee.

clue.text: Bradbury's line

definitions.note: the author's first name, so the possessive stands for 'Bradbury's own first name'
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the given name of the science-fiction writer who wrote Fahrenheit 451
second meaning: a straight line extending from a point, as in geometry or a beam of light

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a quotation from a book; instead it is the writer's first name and a geometric term.
explanation.definitionFit: Ray Bradbury was the American novelist, and in geometry a half-line starting at a point carries the same name.

clue.text: The Flight from the Enchanter finally — it's a novel

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters take a new order
finally points to the very end of the word just before it

parts.note: the last letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reviewer remarks that Iris Murdoch's The Flight from the Enchanter is, at last, a real novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Flight from the Enchanter is Iris Murdoch's second novel; 'novel' looks like the noun but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps can be called a stair, the word used for a whole staircase as well as a single step.

clue.text: I'm inexperienced at acting — I will get in a state!

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so the letter goes inside the other letters

parts.note: a virgin is a complete novice
taken as written
A is a standard abbreviation for acting

explanation.surface: A nervous novice actor fears getting into a terrible state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A state' sounds like panic, but it is a US state; Virginia is also Virginia Woolf, the 5 referred to elsewhere in the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The American Commonwealth on the Atlantic coast, named for Elizabeth I, is one of the fifty member states of the union.

clue.text: One trace of the natural history of creation found in Chambers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a single remaining mark or sign of something

definitions.text: of the natural history of creation found in Chambers
definitions.note: completes the book title Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, one of whose vestiges is the answer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: one of the ... in the title of Robert Chambers's anonymous 1844 book on evolution

explanation.surface: A single clue about how life began has turned up in a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers looks like the dictionary or rooms; it is Robert Chambers, whose Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation anticipated Darwin.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestige is a small remaining sign of something that once existed, and the word is singular of the book's opening noun.

clue.text: Let go wildly in intricate trio in this opera

indicators.note: in places one jumbled group inside the other
doing something wildly means doing it without order, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: intricate means tangled and complicated, so this group of letters is rearranged too

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Three singers in a complex ensemble let rip in an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's tragic work about a hunchbacked court jester, famed for its quartet and La donna è mobile, bears this title.

clue.text: Role for Nicole Kidman to render with little sign of hesitation

parts.note: to render a text into another language is to translate it
er is the short sound people make when hesitating

explanation.surface: An actress has to deliver her part with barely any hesitation.
explanation.walkthrough: Kidman starred in the 2005 thriller The Interpreter, playing a UN translator.
explanation.definitionFit: She played a United Nations translator in Sydney Pollack's thriller, a part whose job title is also the film's name.

clue.text: Hammett's continental detective in heartless stories mingling variant elements

indicators.note: in puts the detective inside the jumbled letters
mingling mixes things together, so the remaining letters are jumbled
without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written before its middle letter goes
Dashiell Hammett's nameless private eye is the Continental Op

explanation.surface: Dashiell Hammett's detective is mixed up in some soulless tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental' looks like geography, but it belongs to the name of Hammett's agency operative from his 1920s pulp stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Isotopes are forms of a chemical element differing in neutron number, so they are versions of the same element.

clue.text: Those corny parts of work by 5

parts.note: they is a pronoun standing for those people
ears are the grain-bearing heads of corn

explanation.surface: Those trite passages come from a book by Virginia Woolf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corny' suggests trite writing, but here it means belonging to corn. 5 is VIRGINIA, as in Virginia Woolf.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's 1937 family-saga novel, following the Pargiters over half a century, carries this title.

clue.text: Thomas Mann's good red, which may nevertheless cause this

definitions.note: the whole phrase points to the stomach upset that cheap wine can cause

parts.note: gut is the German for good, Mann's language
rot is the German for red, carried over from Mann

explanation.surface: Even a decent red wine from Germany can still leave you with a bad stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Mann wrote in German, so both words are translated into German.
explanation.definitionFit: Gut-rot is informal for a stomach ache or for rough cheap alcohol that brings one on, the result of drinking too much.

clue.text: Ad hoc?

parts.note: surface reading: the Latin phrase for something improvised for a particular purpose
setter's reading: Latin hoc means this, so this is an ad, a broadcast advertisement

explanation.walkthrough: The familiar Latin phrase is split: 'ad' is an advertisement and 'hoc' means 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: A paid advertisement on television or radio is called by this noun, which also means profit-making.

clue.text: Mary's confused about day permit for Clarissa

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the next ones
confused means muddled, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
D is the standard abbreviation for day
to permit something is to allow it

explanation.surface: A muddled Mary is getting a day pass sorted out for her friend Clarissa.
explanation.walkthrough: Clarissa is not a second woman beside Mary but the heroine of Virginia Woolf's novel, the 5 of this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa is the first name of the title heroine of Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel, who gives a party in London.

clue.text: What 5 wanted: her 25 —

parts.note: surface reading: an unfinished account of Woolf's wish for something of her own
setter's reading: fill the gap in the title of Woolf's essay arguing a woman writer needs a private space and money

explanation.walkthrough: 5 is VIRGINIA (Woolf) and 25 is OWN, so the phrase is her famous essay title A ___ of One's Own.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's 1929 essay argues that a woman needs money and a private chamber in order to write fiction.

clue.text: Saxon acquaintance of 5

parts.note: surface reading: an Anglo-Saxon, someone of old English stock
setter's reading: Saxon is the first name of a Bloomsbury Group member who knew Virginia Woolf

explanation.walkthrough: Saxon looks like a nationality; it is the given name of the civil servant and Bloomsbury figure, a friend of the Woolfs.
explanation.definitionFit: Saxon Sydney-Turner was a Cambridge friend of Thoby Stephen and part of the Bloomsbury circle around Virginia Woolf.

clue.text: One of Saint-Saens's hémiones, and his excellent dance, we hear, coming first

indicators.note: coming first sets the sounded-out dance at the front of the answer
we hear means the words are taken by their sound rather than spelling

parts.note: Saint-Saëns's Danse macabre sets a poem whose death-dance begins 'Zig et zig et zag'
A1 means first-rate, written here with the numeral looking like I

explanation.surface: A wild ass from The Carnival of the Animals is joined by the composer's best dance tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Hémiones is a movement of The Carnival of the Animals depicting wild asses; the dziggetai is the Mongolian wild ass.
explanation.definitionFit: The dziggetai, or kulan, is an Asian wild ass, one of the hemione species portrayed galloping in Saint-Saëns's suite.

clue.text: Camus's play about Latin Imperator primarily destroying Gaul?

parts.note: CA is short for circa, Latin for about

indicators.note: destroying smashes the word apart so its letters are reassembled

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Latin

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is Camus's drama about a Roman emperor laying waste to France?
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus wrote a 1944 drama about the mad Roman emperor, titled with that emperor's nickname.

clue.text: "The Hero in the — is unsuccessful, and by no means a Match for his Enemies" (Joseph Addison, Spectator)

definitions.text: "The Hero in the — is unsuccessful, and by no means a Match for his Enemies" (Joseph Addison, Spectator)

parts.words: "The Hero in the — is unsuccessful, and by no means a Match for his Enemies"
parts.note: surface reading: a critic complaining of a weak hero who fails against his foes
setter's reading: Addison's Spectator essays criticised Milton's epic, whose hero Adam is defeated

explanation.walkthrough: A gap-fill quotation: Addison wrote a long series of Spectator papers on Milton's epic.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's epic poem about the fall of Adam and Eve was the subject of Addison's famous series of Spectator critiques.

clue.text: Novel reputed to have broken through like White Teeth?

indicators.note: novel means new, so the next word's letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A novel is said to have been a breakthrough, like Zadie Smith's White Teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: White Teeth is Zadie Smith's debut novel, but here the words just mean teeth coming through the gums.
explanation.definitionFit: New teeth are said to erupt when they break through the gum, so the verb means burst out.

clue.text: E. Lear's replaced by latter-day cartoonist

indicators.note: replaced means put back in different positions, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, punctuation dropped

explanation.surface: Edward Lear, the Victorian nonsense artist, has been succeeded by a modern cartoonist.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Searle drew the St Trinian's schoolgirls and illustrated the Molesworth books.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Searle was a twentieth-century British illustrator famous for St Trinian's, a modern successor to Lear's comic drawing.

clue.text: Larkin's character judgement initially poor

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
ill means poorly, in bad health

explanation.surface: A critic's opening verdict on Larkin's characterisation is that it is weak.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Larkin's first novel, Jill, is named after an imaginary girl its hero invents.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkin's 1946 Oxford novel takes its title from the fictional schoolgirl that its student hero John Kemp dreams up.

clue.text: Now named after Milton, it was new when Gissing wrote about it

definitions.text: Now named after Milton, it was new when Gissing wrote about it

parts.note: surface reading: some place recently renamed in honour of the poet

parts.words: it was new when Gissing wrote about it
parts.note: setter's reading: George Gissing's novel puts the word New before the old name of this London street of hack writers

explanation.walkthrough: The London street of hack writers was renamed Milton Street in 1830; Gissing's 1891 novel is New Grub Street.
explanation.definitionFit: The old London thoroughfare synonymous with impoverished hack writers became Milton Street and gave Gissing's novel its title.

clue.text: Gracious, like Simon's charity

definitions.note: describes the charity, an adjective like the answer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word in the title of the musical ... Charity, with a book by Neil Simon

explanation.walkthrough: Simon is Neil Simon, who wrote the book of the 1966 Broadway musical Sweet Charity.
explanation.definitionFit: A gracious person is kindly and charming, and the adjective also opens the title of Neil Simon's Broadway musical.

clue.text: Defeat and endlessly rout one of Roald Dahl's practical jokers

parts.note: Mr and Mrs Twit play nasty tricks on each other in Dahl's The Twits

explanation.surface: Beat a prankster from a Roald Dahl story and keep routing him.

clue.text: Numerically appropriate version of 12 by Cunningham; or much shorter version of 9?

definitions.text: Numerically appropriate version of 12 by Cunningham

parts.words: Numerically appropriate version of 12 by Cunningham

clue.text: Lawrence's short story about Mrs Johnson

second meaning: the nickname of the wife of US President Lyndon B. Johnson

clue.text: Miss Whitefield taken in by this eccentric roué initially?
